name: Electric toothbrush whitening heads

lead: Whitening heads swap onto an electric toothbrush to scrub off coffee, tea and other surface stain, giving teeth a brighter look.

The polishing bristles, cups or pads remove stain from the outer surface mechanically. They do not change the tooth's inner colour. No studies of these heads specifically were found; a 2014 Cochrane review found powered brushes in general remove somewhat more plaque and reduce gum inflammation more than manual brushes.

paras: People fit the head to a compatible handle and use it as their regular daily brush, often alongside whitening toothpaste. Brighter shade from stain removal shows over days to weeks, and heads are normally replaced about every three months.
Heavy brushing pressure can wear enamel and irritate gums, and many powered brushes have pressure sensors for this reason. They cannot lighten intrinsic discolouration, which needs bleaching.

angle.text: Whitening heads on powered brushes lift coffee, tea and other surface stain for a brighter smile. Polishing cups and pads scrub stain off the outer enamel, though they do not bleach the tooth. No trials of these specific heads were found.

lead: Electric toothbrush whitening heads are replacement brush heads marketed for powered toothbrushes to remove surface stains and make teeth look whiter. They typically differ from standard heads in bristle layout or a polishing cup or pad. People use them to keep the visible shade of their teeth brighter day to day, since stained teeth are a common reason people feel their smile looks dull.

Wikipedia describes extrinsic stain as sitting on the tooth surface and coming largely from smoking, tannin-rich drinks such as coffee, tea and red wine, and certain foods, and says it can often be removed by cleaning, while intrinsic stain lies within the tooth and is the main target of bleaching [1]. Whitening heads address the first kind.

Electric toothbrushes in general are described as removing more plaque and reducing gum inflammation than manual brushes in a 2014 Cochrane review, though the review authors questioned the clinical importance of the difference [2]. No published trial has tested whitening heads against standard heads.

paras: Powered toothbrushes are oscillating-rotating, sonic (typically 200 to 400 Hz) or ultrasonic [2]. Manufacturers sell heads labelled for whitening, often with polishing elements, and many sonic brushes include a whitening mode alongside daily care, sensitive teeth and tongue cleaning modes [2].
Electric brushes date to Tomlinson Moseley's Motodent patent in 1937 and Philippe-Guy Woog's Broxodent in 1954, with the first ultrasonic brush patented in the US in 1992 [2].

sections.h: What brushing can and cannot change
paras: Surface stains from coffee, tea, red wine and tobacco can be reduced by cleaning, while intrinsic discolouration within the tooth is not removable by cleaning and is what bleaching targets [1]. Whitening toothpastes, which use higher amounts of abrasives and detergents, can lighten tooth colour by one or two shades with continued use, according to Wikipedia [1]. Wikipedia also notes that overly abrasive whitening toothpastes can harm dental tissue [1].
Brushing too hard can damage enamel and gums, and some brushes include pressure sensors [2]. Manufacturers advise replacing heads about every three months [2].

No studies found specific to whitening heads. Broader research on electric versus manual brushing is summarised in a 2014 Cochrane review, which reported plaque reductions of 11 percent after one to three months and 21 percent after three months, and gum-inflammation reductions of 6 and 11 percent; only oscillating-rotating brushes consistently showed a statistically significant benefit [2].
